newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europeans prefer the couch to the cinema.
newsitem.headline: Europeans prefer the couch to the cinema.

text.p: European Union citizens have become couch potatoes, preferring to watch television and videos rather than go to the cinema, a new European Union report showed on Monday.
"Television and video dominate the entertainment scene in the EU -- with a huge increase in choice in the last decade," the EU's statistical office Eurostat said in a statement.

In 1994, 95.7 percent of EU households had at least one television set, 58.6 percent had a video recorder, 21.6 percent subscribed to cable television and 10.1 percent were connected to satellite dishes, the study said.
While in 1981 the average EU citizen went to the cinema three times a year, in 1994 they only went 1.8 times a year.
And while receipts from sales and rentals of video cassettes brought in 4.7 billion Ecus ($5.6 billion), cinema revenue from gross box office receipts was only three billion Ecus ($3.6 billion).
In 1994 the number of full length feature films produced in the 15-nation EU also dropped to 519, its lowest level since 1983 when there were 583.
Of those, 22 percent came from France, 18.3 from Italy, 13.5 from Britain, 11.6 percent from Germany and 8.3 percent from Spain.
But the study said all was not entirely dark for the cinema, which despite its decline is regaining popularity compared to the early 1990s.
Eurostat said it put the increasing popularity of television down to greater choice -- the number of EU television channels with national coverage almost doubled to 88 from 47 between 1988 and 1994.
While cable television is increasingly popular, it is very rare in southern member states like Portugal, Italy and Greece, where less than one percent of households have it.
In Belgium and the Netherlands on the other hand over 91 percent of households have subscribed.
